Vulnerability of primitive human placental trophoblast to Zika virus

Let me attempt an explanation for those not familiar with some of the special language. The trophoblast is part of the early cell wall of a fertilized egg, which proceeds to attach itself to the endometrium lining (approximately day six after fertilization). After this process begins, syncytiotrophoblasts connect with the embryo forming an outer layer of nutrient circulation. This, being a layer of blood connection, provides the avenue for attack from Zika. Lysis is the process through which cell membranes are broken down by viral infection. The embryo is, therefore, most vulnerable to this infection before the "hairy" (villus) protective membrane of the trophoblast can develop. This would seem to imply that early infection of Zika would destroy the embryo before development, as by one or two months the cell should be well protected.

What is most surprising by this is the fact the less virulent strain of Zika has more success invading the undeveloped cell, as well as that it's considered benign for pregnancy.
